entities.summary:
Bartolomeo Vivarini was a prominent Italian painter of the early Renaissance, born in Venice around 1450, who spent his career painting frescoes in various churches and altarpieces across the region. 

 Vivarini's most famous works include the frescoes in the San Zeno Maggiore in Venice, the San Zeno Nuovo in Treviso, and the San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, showcasing his mastery of color and composition.

 Through his paintings, Vivarini contributed to the development of the Venetian school of painting, which was characterized by its use of vibrant colors and emotive figures. His work also had a significant impact on the art of the region, influencing the styles of later artists such as Titian and Tintoretto.

 Vivarini's artistic legacy extends beyond his individual works, as he played a crucial role in shaping the artistic identity of the Venetian Republic during the 15th and 16th centuries. His paintings continue to be celebrated for their beauty, emotion, and historical significance, offering a glimpse into the cultural and artistic landscape of early Renaissance Italy.

 Vivarini's work can be seen in various museums and galleries, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington D.C., the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City, and the Gallerie dell'Accademia in Venice.

 Vivarini's artistic style was heavily influenced by his contemporaries, including the great masters of the Venetian school, and his work can be seen in many of the iconic churches and piazzas of Venice, such as St. Mark's Square and the Rialto Bridge.

 Vivarini's artistic output was also shaped by the cultural and economic changes of the time, as the Venetian Republic was undergoing a period of significant growth and expansion during the 15th century.
